items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Anyway, Art called me, said he had this gig at the Half Note for two weeks.

ctx.x: How did you come to be in Art's group?

I'd done a duo record with Jim Hall at the Playboy Club sometime before that, I think. Art was in town and put together a band to go into the Half-Note which was on Spring and Hudson in those days, 1963. Walter Perkins who I knew, from working these little gigs around town … down at the Birdland, jam session Monday nights, Five Spot, Monday night jam sessions. I would see these guys. I didn't know them but I would see them, you know. Actually, you know, that was a very closed circuit at that time – the jam…
Now it was during that period that Miles came by.

items.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He had Cannonball, J.J., Ron Carter, Joe Zawinul, Mel Lewis and myself; we were the judges.

ctx.x: There’s a classic pianist named Friedrich Gulda, and I ran into him in Berlin. On my off night, I went to a concert he was playing. He was playing a concert and had Ron Carter and Tootie Heath. The first part of the concert he’d play classic Mozart and all that, and then the second half was jazz. I had known him from a time that he visited here in New York, and I was talking to him on the break, and he told me about this thing that was going on, this competition. He asked me if I wanted to be one of the judges,…
What would you do in those ten days?

items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: I saw Horace play there with Art Farmer and Clifford Jordan

ctx.x: How did your professors feel about that? Or wasn’t it even an issue for them?

Well most of them didn’t really care. I went to class on time and did the homework. Some of them didn’t care for that kind of music so they didn’t like what I did in classes, and the school did not encourage a jazz profile. And the strange thing is at that time there was the Eastman Theater, there was a show called “Jazz for Moderns” that would travel throughout the country. And they played at the Eastman Theater, it was a wonderful auditorium, it seated maybe 2,000 people. And they had great bands going all…
force in music, it’s hard to understand how a classical institution would continue to ignore its presence.
